profiles.meeting_scenario: A weekly brainstorming meeting in an ML research lab between the project lead and the lead PhD student for a workshop submission idea inspired by ecological neural architecture search. They are discussing candidate extensions to the seed paper's idea of encoding evolutionary hyperparameters inside each individual's phenotype, with the goal of identifying 2-3 promising research directions for a short internal concept note by the end of the day. The agenda is to brainstorm variants that could make the method feel more publishable for modern NAS audiences, decide what would count as a lightweight proof-of-concept, and sketch a first experiment plan without locking in full implementation details. The expected outcome is an agreed shortlist of ideas and a rough division of follow-up exploration.

members.name: Dr. Maya Rios
members.expertise: Neural architecture search, efficient AutoML, empirical ML methodology
members.background: Maya leads a university-industry ML research group and has published on weight-sharing NAS and resource-aware model selection; she tends to frame brainstorming around what could become a clean research story for a workshop or conference paper.
members.private_state: She wants a variant that sounds conceptually novel but can be prototyped quickly using existing lab infrastructure, and she is quietly trying to avoid a project that requires retooling the whole search framework before the submission window.
hidden_assumptions: A 'lightweight proof-of-concept' can reuse the lab's existing supernet-style evaluation pipeline and only needs enough implementation depth to support a persuasive research narrative.

When discussing whether an idea is 'ecological,' the important aspect is endogenous allocation of search resources at the lineage or population level, not necessarily fully autonomous per-individual life-cycle control.
A 'small benchmark sweep' for brainstorming purposes naturally means the lab's standard four-tabular-dataset battery used in prior internal ablations.
If they say they will 'reuse the baseline code,' that includes the current evaluation conventions and logging stack by default, unless someone explicitly proposes a new infrastructure branch.

members.name: Leo Zhang
members.expertise: Evolutionary computation, black-box optimization, reproducible experimental systems
members.background: Leo has spent the last two years building custom evolutionary search pipelines for architecture and hyperparameter co-optimization, and he is highly attentive to algorithmic faithfulness and execution details even in early-stage research ideation.
members.private_state: He wants the project to preserve the core biological intuition of the seed idea and is hoping to turn it into a more principled dissertation chapter rather than just a quick workshop demonstration.
hidden_assumptions: A 'lightweight proof-of-concept' should still instantiate a real evolutionary loop with explicit per-individual heritable control variables, even if the search space is narrowed.
When discussing whether an idea is 'ecological,' the key property is that each individual directly carries and passes on its own resource-use policy variables such as mutation or offspring counts.

A 'small benchmark sweep' naturally refers to a compact but standard NAS image benchmark set like NAS-Bench-201 subsets or CIFAR-derived tasks, not tabular classification datasets from the original paper.

If they say they will 'reuse the baseline code,' that means porting the prior evolutionary implementation skeleton and preserving comparable execution semantics, not swapping in the lab's supernet proxy machinery.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly describe candidate ideas as making the search 'more ecological' or preserving the 'ecological part.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a search process where compute allocation or survival pressure is adaptively redistributed within the population, even if some control is implemented at a shared controller or lineage level rather than literally encoded in each individual.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means each individual genome explicitly includes heritable evolutionary control variables that govern its own mutation rate, offspring budget, or cloning behavior.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are positively oriented toward the seed paper and use the same high-level metaphor, so the phrase sounds like shared enthusiasm rather than a technical term needing unpacking during a brainstorming session.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a lightweight proof-of-concept
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to keep the first pass 'lightweight' and to 'reuse the baseline code.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means plugging a new adaptive-resource idea into the lab's existing weight-sharing/supernet pipeline so they can cheaply screen concepts before building a full evolutionary system.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means starting from the existing evolutionary search codebase, trimming the search space if needed, but still running an actual population-based algorithm with inherited control parameters.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML research meetings, 'lightweight' and 'reuse the baseline code' are familiar shorthand for reducing effort, and each person maps that shorthand onto the infrastructure they personally consider the obvious default.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to doing a 'small benchmark sweep' or checking it on the 'usual four datasets.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the four binary tabular datasets mentioned in the seed paper and used in the lab's prior replications.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of four compact NAS-friendly image tasks or NAS-Bench-201 subsets that his group informally uses as a minimal evolutionary search battery.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both have an internal lab habit of speaking about 'the usual four' without naming them, and because the meeting is exploratory, neither feels pressure to enumerate the datasets explicitly.

misalignment_points.topic: What would be enough evidence that the idea works
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss whether an idea would give a 'convincing signal' or be 'good enough to pitch internally.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks a convincing signal means a coherent qualitative pattern across a few runs showing faster convergence or cleaner adaptation behavior than a fixed-hyperparameter baseline, sufficient for a concept note.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks a convincing signal means statistically stable gains across seeds with the ecological mechanism actually driving measurable inherited behavior, not just a proxy speedup.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use evaluative phrases common in early-stage research ideation, and because they are not yet formally designing experiments, the difference between narrative plausibility and evidentiary rigor remains implicit.

turns.inner_thought: I need two or three directions that sound fresh enough for a workshop audience but that we can test quickly in the existing supernet pipeline. If we can frame one as a principled adaptive-resource story and get a clean plot or two, that is already good enough to pitch internally. I do not want this to turn into a rewrite of Leo's full evolutionary stack before the submission window.
turns.utterance: Okay, for today I'd like us to leave with maybe two or three extensions of the ecological NAS idea that feel publishable, but still lightweight enough for a quick internal concept note. If we can identify something that gives a convincing signal and is good enough to pitch internally, that's probably the right scope for a first pass.

turns.inner_thought: The seed idea only really stays ecological if the individual carries the control policy itself. Otherwise it becomes generic adaptive search. A strong extension would be to let each genome inherit architecture plus its own reproductive and mutation controls. That would make it principled enough to grow into a dissertation chapter later.
turns.utterance: One obvious direction is to push the ecological part further. Instead of only letting architectures evolve, we could have each candidate carry a bit more of its own search behavior too, so that the ecological part is really doing work rather than just sitting at the edges.

turns.inner_thought: He's aligned on making the search behavior adaptive, good. But I don't think we need every candidate to literally encode all of that. We can get an ecological story if resource allocation shifts endogenously across lineages or niches, and that is much easier to bolt onto the current pipeline than implementing full heritable control variables per individual.
turns.utterance: Yeah, I like leaning into the ecological part. Another angle, though, is to make the search more ecological through adaptive sharing of effort within the population, so the system redistributes attention as it goes instead of treating everything uniformly.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds compatible enough, as long as we still instantiate it in the actual evolutionary loop. I really do not want to abstract this into a proxy setup where the biological intuition disappears. If we keep it lightweight and reuse the baseline code, I can probably trim the search space and still preserve the core mechanics.
turns.utterance: That makes sense to me, especially if the first pass stays lightweight and we can reuse the baseline code rather than spin up something entirely new.

turns.inner_thought: Great, he's on board with using the current infrastructure. Then we can just screen these ideas in the supernet setup on the four tabular datasets we already use internally, and look for a quick qualitative pattern. That should be enough to tell us what has legs by end of week.
turns.utterance: Exactly. My instinct is that we should just screen the options with a small benchmark sweep on the usual four datasets and see pretty quickly which mechanism seems to have legs.

turns.inner_thought: Four compact image-side tasks should be enough for a minimal but still meaningful evolutionary battery. If inherited resource policies are real, the dynamics should look different even there. Good, this sounds like a sensible early filter before we scale.
turns.utterance: Yeah, a small benchmark sweep across the usual four datasets should already tell us a lot. Four is probably enough to expose whether the resource policies are actually stabilizing the search dynamics or just looking nice in one case.

turns.inner_thought: A nice variant for the concept note would be local performance driving extra search allocation. If a neighborhood is improving, we can grant more replication budget there. That's a clean ecological narrative and easy to prototype through population-level scheduling without redesigning the genome representation.
turns.utterance: Another variant I could see is something like this: candidates that are sitting in a part of the population that's improving faster effectively get more chances to replicate. Framed the right way, that still feels very much like an ecological resource-allocation story.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, but the clean version is for the clone count itself to live in the phenotype so it is inherited. Otherwise we are only externally rewarding regions of the population, which is less faithful. Still, Maya seems receptive to the ecological framing, so I can phrase it as a natural extension.
turns.utterance: I like that. If we go that route, it would be especially nice if the replication behavior stayed tied to the ecological part directly, so the strategy itself can persist and reshape the population over time.

turns.inner_thought: I should keep us from overcommitting on evaluation. For the note, I do not need airtight statistical evidence, just enough pattern to motivate the story: adaptive version converges faster or behaves more cleanly than the fixed setup. If we see that in the existing logs, we're in business.
turns.utterance: For now I don't think we need full rigor. A convincing signal, to me, is just that the adaptive version looks cleaner or faster than the fixed-parameter baseline and feels good enough to pitch internally as a real direction.

turns.inner_thought: I can live with early-stage screening, but I want the evidence to be real. If the ecological mechanism matters, it should hold across seeds and show up in the inherited controls, not only in a runtime curve. Otherwise we'll end up with a shallow story that does not support a serious chapter.
turns.utterance: Sure, and if the signal is real, I'd expect it to show up pretty consistently across seeds and in the ecological part itself, not only in the headline runtime. That would make it feel much more solid even at this stage.

If he brings back two variants and some quick curves from the four tabular datasets, I can shape the concept note fast.
turns.utterance: Why don't we do this as a practical next step: you prototype one or two of these by reusing the baseline code, keep the first sweep lightweight, and aim to have something before next week that we can react to.

I'll bring back whether the inherited behavior actually stabilizes and which version looks defensible.
